meta.description: This one has a citation — Rita Dove’s 1999 Time profile of Rosa Parks. What that citation does and does not establish.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I did not get on the bus to get arrested. I got on the bus to go home'?
meta.ogDescription: Wikiquote traces it to Rita Dove’s 1999 Time profile. That is a secondary source, and a poet’s prose — worth knowing before you quote it.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: This line is in better shape than most quotations pinned on Rosa Parks: Wikiquote carries it in its sourced section, not the unsourced list, and cites Rita Dove’s profile of Parks in Time of 14 June 1999. Two things keep it short of verified. The citation is to a magazine essay written forty-four years after the event, not to Parks’s own book or a transcript; and the essay itself could not be retrieved from this session, so we have not seen the sentence in its original setting or confirmed whether Dove presents it as Parks’s words.
answer.confidenceText: Better sourced than most Parks quotations — but the trail ends at a magazine profile, not at Parks.

source.excerpt: I did not get on the bus to get arrested. I got on the bus to go home.
trail: Wikiquote carries it as sourced, not unsourced. On the Rosa Parks page ↗ it sits in the main quotations list with a citation: Rita Dove, “Rosa Parks: Her simple act of protest galvanized America’s civil rights revolution,” Time, 14 June 1999. It is not on the talk page’s unsourced list ↗, where several other popular Parks lines sit.

We could not read the essay. Time’s site is refused by this session’s network, and so is the Wayback Machine, so the sentence has not been confirmed in print. We cannot tell from here whether the old link Wikiquote gives still resolves, and we are not going to guess. Everything below rests on Wikiquote’s citation rather than on the article itself, and we would rather say so than imply a reading we did not do.

Worth knowing who Rita Dove is. She is a former US Poet Laureate who, in that same year, published On the Bus with Rosa Parks ↗, a book of poems about Parks. A sentence relayed through a poet’s profile is not thereby wrong — but it is the kind of setting where narration and quotation blur, and that is a reason to keep this at “attributed.”

Her papers do not contain the phrase. A full-text search of the Rosa Parks Papers ↗ for “got on the bus to go home” returns nothing, so the Library of Congress holdings add no independent confirmation.

source.rightsNote: No rights status is asserted, and none of this is public domain. We could not determine which, so we assert neither.

author.name: Rosa Parks
author.kicker: The woman who would not move
author.heading: About Rosa Parks
author.metaLine: 1913–2005 · American civil rights activist · Montgomery, Alabama
author.bio: Rosa Louise McCauley Parks was a seamstress and long-serving NAACP secretary in Montgomery, Alabama, whose refusal to give up her bus seat on 1 December 1955 set off the Montgomery bus boycott. Congress later called her the Mother of the Modern-Day Civil Rights Movement, a title that has had the odd side effect of attracting inspirational sentences she never demonstrably wrote. She published an autobiography, Rosa Parks: My Story, with James Haskins in 1992, and her papers are held at the Library of Congress.

context.heading: Why it is quoted so often
lead: The appeal of the line is that it deflates the monument. The bus boycott turned Parks into a symbol, and this sentence puts her back on a Thursday evening commute, going home from a day’s work as a seamstress at Montgomery Fair — the arrest something done to her, not a performance she staged.

That is also a reason to handle it carefully. It is exactly the sort of neat, quotable deflation that gets tightened in the retelling, and the earliest citation anyone offers is a magazine essay from 1999 rather than anything Parks published herself.
context.pull: The trail ends at a 1999 magazine profile — which is further than most Parks quotations get, and still not Parks.

sourcesVerified.claim: The English Wikiquote article "Rosa Parks" carries, in its sourced quotations list, "I did not get on the bus to get arrested. I got on the bus to go home.", cited to Rita Dove, "Rosa Parks: Her simple act of protest galvanized America's civil rights revolution," Time (1999-06-14).
This sentence is NOT among the quotations listed under "Unsourced" on the talk page of the English Wikiquote article "Rosa Parks".
Wikipedia records "On the Bus with Rosa Parks" as a 1999 book of poems by Rita Dove about Rosa Parks.
A full-text search of the Library of Congress Rosa Parks Papers collection for the exact phrase "got on the bus to go home" returns zero results, against a validated search.

The English Wikiquote article "Rosa Parks" lists roughly a dozen quotations that each carry a named source (Rosa Parks: My Story p. 116; an NPR interview of 1992; a 1995 Washington speech; Theoharis's The Rebellious Life of Mrs. Rosa Parks).
The talk page of the English Wikiquote article "Rosa Parks" carries a section headed "Unsourced" listing quotations attributed to Parks that editors could not tie to a publication.

Wikiquote's sourced section gives "People always said that I didn't give up my seat because I was tired, but that isn't true... the only tired I was, was tired of giving in," citing Rosa Parks: My Story, p. 116, Rosa Parks and James Haskins (1992).

The Internet Archive holds a scan of "Rosa Parks: My Story" catalogued to Parks (1913-2005) and published by Puffin Books, dated 1999 in the item metadata; the full text is lending-restricted and could not be read or searched.

Wikipedia records Rosa Louise McCauley Parks as an American civil rights activist, 1913-2005, best known for her 1955 refusal to move from her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, which sparked the Montgomery bus boycott.
